item.title: Why Medicare’s 2027 physician pay changes worry some specialists
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on Medicare changes affecting specialists, with real-world impact on patient care.

Podiatrist Heather McGuire always wanted to serve in a clinic in her hometown of Ventura, Calif. Fifteen years after she opened her practice, she is realizing her dream in the community that raised her, treating suburbanites and agricultural workers with diabetes on Medicare.

But McGuire believes that dream may be ending.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ recent update to how Medicare pays physicians cut the payment rate for certain services provided on the same day by 20% when it’s provided by the same physician or practice. McGuire’s practice already operates on extremely thin margins, and she recently shelved a plan to hire another doctor to improve the practice’s exceedingly long wait times.

It could worsen Medicare recipients’ access to specialist care in Ventura, too. Last week, the podiatrist saw a new patient, a woman in her 80s, who waited two and a half months for an appointment to get her heel pain checked out. When the patient arrived, McGuire found that it wasn’t just heel pain. The woman had also developed an ulcer on her other foot during her long appointment wait. Left unchecked, an ulcer in someone with diabetes can lead to amputations.

“I would be paid 20% less for providing potentially lifesaving or limb-saving treatment care for that wound because she also had another complaint at the same visit,” McGuire said.

Podiatrists, dermatologists, and otolaryngologists are among the biggest losers with this change, according to an analysis by the American Medical Association, an advocacy group for physicians. Opponents of the policy, including the AMA, say it will force patients to return for separate appointments, raise out-of-pocket costs, and increase wait times, especially for patients in rural areas who have less access to specialists.

“If you’re running your own small group practice [accepting Medicare patients], can you still financially do that?” said Miranda Franco, a senior policy adviser at the law firm Holland & Knight. “Or are you going to start thinking about, you know, maybe consolidating into a hospital system or private equity to defray some of that financial loss?”

These billing code changes are an attempt to modernize Medicare and reduce administrative burden, a CMS spokesperson said. It is part of the agency’s broader shift away from specialist care and the fee-for-service model, and one of many reimbursement challenges that specialists are contending with.

Not everyone is against the change in payment rates for services rendered on the same day. The Medicare Payment Advisory Commission, a nonpartisan group that advises Congress on Medicare, supports it, saying it will remove redundancies and duplicative payments. The Justice Department has also found multiple instances of providers committing fraud through this billing code.

The cuts to payment rates for same-day services were slated to be 50% when first proposed in 2018, before backlash from physicians and patients softened the blow. Under the final rule, effective Jan. 1, 2027, Medicare will pay for the highest-valued same-day service at 100%, then reduce payment for each additional service rendered on the same day by 20% when physicians perform evaluations and other routine outpatient services. CMS argues the lowered rate is justified because providers use less resources — for patient registration, scheduling, and support, for example — when patients are seen and treated on the same day at the same practice.

Amy Hunsberger, a lawyer with Manatt, a legal advisory and consultancy, said the cuts are partly motivated by the statutory requirement that physician payments cannot increase without Congressional approval, forcing Medicare to cut back on expenses as the agency spends more on health care costs.

“You have a balloon that has so much air in it, and when you reduce payment in one area of services, you’re squeezing the balloon on one side, and it pushes payments out to the rest of the balloon,” said Hunsberger. “This balloon is not updated for inflation and relies on continual, almost annual congressional bailouts to get clinicians to some semblance of reasonable payment.”

Because these policy changes apply to the number of claims relating to health care services rendered on the same day and to any specific specialty, it’s unclear how they will impact Medicare beneficiaries. The American Parkinson Disease Association said patients with Parkinson’s disease are worried that it could impact their ability to get outpatient Botox injections that are critical for relieving pain.

McGuire estimates that the policy change will decrease her profits by 6%. The policy goes into effect on Jan. 1. She doesn’t know how much longer her practice will last.

“There are times where I ask myself if I should just close up shop and call it a day, and go find a job at Trader Joe’s or Starbucks, where I can have a reliable income,” she said. “If it wasn’t for the fact that medicine has always been a calling for me and the joy it brings me to take care of patients, I probably would have done that already. But I’m also getting to the point where I don’t think this is financially viable and a long-term solution.”

item.title: 2000 to 2024 saw decrease in age-adjusted stroke death rate in U.S.
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed analysis of stroke death rates with clear presentation of trends and demographics.

2000 to 2024 saw decrease in age-adjusted stroke death rate in U.S.

During 2000 to 2024, there was a decrease in the age-adjusted stroke death rate, although rates increased among certain groups in the most recent trend periods, according to research published in the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

Xin Tong, M.P.H., from the CDC in Atlanta, and colleagues examined 25-year trends in stroke death rates among U.S. adults across age, sex and geographic areas using mortality data from the 2000 to 2024 National Vital Statistics System.

The researchers observed a decline in the age-adjusted stroke death rate among U.S. adults during 2000 to 2024, from 81.4 to 51.9 per 100,000 (average annual percentage change, −2.0%), with decreasing trends across all age groups, sexes, U.S. Census Bureau regions and U.S. jurisdictions (apart from Delaware).

The overall rates decreased during 2000 to 2009, remained stable during 2009 to 2018, increased during 2018 to 2021 and decreased during 2021 to 2024, with annual percentage changes of −5.2% during 2000 to 2009, 4.0% during 2018 to 2021 and −2.4% during 2021 to 2024. Among adults aged 35 to 44 years, those aged 85 years and older, women, residents of the Midwest and South U.S. Census Bureau regions, and residents of 12 U.S. jurisdictions, rates increased during the most recent trend periods.

"Recent stalled or reversed declines in stroke death rates among younger adults, women, and residents of some U.S. Census Bureau regions and several U.S. jurisdictions indicate uneven progress," the authors write.

Publication details

Xin Tong et al., Stroke Death Rates Among Adults Aged ≥18 Years — United States, 2000–2024, MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (2026). DOI: 10.15585/mmwr.mm7545a1

item.title: One body, two systems: Integrating dental and medical care dramatically improves dental follow-up
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Innovative approach to improving dental care through integration with medical care, with clear benefits.

One body, two systems: Integrating dental and medical care dramatically improves dental follow-up

In the United States, medical and dental care are traditionally separate. Care is provided in separate locations, recorded in separate systems and paid for via separate methods.

But a new study has found that bringing the two systems together dramatically improves kids' odds of dental follow-up, creating new opportunities to prevent oral disease.

Integrating dental care with medical care resulted in 30%–60% greater odds of continuing dental care, and patients at an integrated clinic had significantly better dental health.

"We asked: Are kids more likely to return for dental care in this integrated environment?" says Jeri Bullock, D.D.S., M.S., associate dean for clinical affairs at the University of Utah School of Dentistry and first author on the study. "We found that yes, they were. Definitely."

The results are published in the Journal of Dental Research.

Care under one roof increases dental checkups and improves health

Researchers compared dental care follow-up between two dental clinics in Salt Lake City: Liberty Elementary Clinic, where medical and dental care are provided by two different organizations with separate health records, and South Main Clinic, where medical and dental care are fully integrated. By tracking over 1,600 pediatric visits to the two clinics, the team found that kids who visited the fully integrated South Main Clinic were 30%–60% more likely to return for a dental appointment within two years.

Importantly, kids who got dental care at South Main tended to have healthier teeth despite demographic differences—such as a trend toward lower socioeconomic status—that often correlate with worse health outcomes. This suggests that an integrated system may lower structural barriers to dental care, helping all children get the care they need.

Researchers suspect that the better oral health of South Main patients is driven by their more frequent dentist appointments.

"The oral health-related quality of life is much higher for patients visiting that site," says Brenda Heaton, Ph.D., associate dean for research at the University of Utah School of Dentistry and senior author on the study. "They're getting the same kind of care at both sites, but because of the model of care delivery, they have better outcomes."

For patients and families used to separate dental care, full medical-dental integration is a big change.

"It's a very unique experience for a patient to be able to get both their medical care and their dental care under the same roof," Heaton says. "Imagine it's a primary care visit for pediatrics, and the kid shares with the physician that they have pain in their mouth. When they check out, the front desk can schedule a dental appointment for them right there at the clinic." Medical and dental health records are also shared on the same electronic system. And if needed, a dentist can walk right down the hall to do a quick consultation during a general checkup.

Dentists and dental researchers have advocated for increased integration into health care systems for years, but the rigorous statistics of the new study make its results especially compelling, the team says. Researchers used multiple parallel methods of data analysis to facilitate direct comparisons between demographically similar patients, allowing them to isolate the effect of medical-dental integration. "It allowed us to really compare apples to apples," Bullock says.

Seeing results in the real world

Bullock adds that the results bear out what she's seen in her own clinical practice at South Main. "I see this day to day," Bullock says. "I know this works; I'm seeing these kids back. I just felt that there was something special. But to actually see it come out in the numbers was really gratifying. I was really excited and proud and felt good as a clinician that what I felt and what I was seeing was true to what the data was saying."

The team warns that the barriers to full medical-dental integration are significant. Bullock notes that effective integration needs a unified electronic health record system, so that dentists and pediatricians can quickly understand a patient's medical needs and provide seamless care. Transitioning to such a system represents a major hurdle for most medical systems.

Still, the researchers are hopeful that their results might help drive greater integration and better patient care, both at University of Utah clinics and more broadly.

"For more than a century, we've treated one body through two disconnected systems," Heaton says. "When medical and dental care work together, we reduce barriers, simplify care for families and create more opportunities to prevent disease before it becomes a larger health problem. My hope is that studies like this help move health care toward models that recognize oral health as an integral part of overall health."

Publication details

J.L. Bullock et al., Integrated Care Improves Continuity of Oral Health Care in Pediatrics, Journal of Dental Research (2026). DOI: 10.1177/00220345261502392

Journal information: Journal of Dental Research

item.title: Electronic health record algorithm can identify drug-resistant epilepsy
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Technical yet accessible explanation of an EHR algorithm for identifying drug-resistant epilepsy.

Electronic health record algorithm can identify drug-resistant epilepsy

An electronic health record (EHR) algorithm can identify people with drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE), according to a study published in the December issue of Epilepsy & Behavior.

Grace B. Simmons, from Columbia University Medical Center in New York City, and colleagues identified people with probable DRE from EHR data using a computable phenotypic algorithm. Two hundred people were randomly sampled for manual chart abstraction.

A total of 3,027 people with probable DRE were identified by the algorithm. The researchers found that 175 (87.5%) of the 200 randomly sampled people had epilepsy; 42% and 11.5% had DRE and epilepsy with undefined drug responsiveness, respectively. More than half of those with DRE (48 of 84; 57.1%) had not initiated presurgical evaluation.

There were associations seen for presurgical evaluation with comorbid mood disorder (odds ratio, 3.88), shorter median time since last epilepsy-related visit and second-to-last epilepsy visit (2.40 versus 6.96 months and 8.76 versus 13.08 months, respectively), and tracking by a surgical coordinator (odds ratio, 46.00). Lower odds of evaluation were seen in association with unknown magnetic resonance imaging classification (odds ratio, 0.04) and generalized seizures (odds ratio, 0.04).

"Over half of people with DRE have not had their candidacy for epilepsy surgery determined or begun presurgical evaluation, and substantial numbers continue to have undefined drug responsiveness despite uncontrolled seizures," the authors write. "Our findings suggest that systematic patient tracking, enhanced care coordination, and streamlined diagnostic pathways should be further investigated."

More information

Grace B. Simmons et al., Status of presurgical evaluation among patients with drug-resistant epilepsy identified with a computable electronic health record algorithm, Epilepsy & Behavior (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.yebeh.2026.111274

item.title: Multidisciplinary intervention improves fatigue for lymphoma survivors
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Study on multidisciplinary intervention for lymphoma survivors with clear outcomes and implications.

Multidisciplinary intervention improves fatigue for lymphoma survivors

For lymphoma survivors with persistent fatigue, a multidisciplinary intervention improves fatigue, and the effect is maintained to six months, according to a study published online Nov. 20 in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.

Synne-Kristin H. Bøhn, Ph.D., from Oslo University Hospital in Norway, and colleagues examined the effects of a multidisciplinary intervention on fatigue among lymphoma survivors with persistent fatigue. Participants were randomly assigned to usual care or a 12-week multidisciplinary intervention, including patient education, physical exercise, a cognitive behavioral therapy–based program and nutritional counseling (75 to each). Total fatigue was assessed using the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire at three months after randomization (T1; primary outcome) and at six and nine months after randomization (T2 and T3; secondary outcomes).

The researchers found that the intervention group reported significantly lower total fatigue at T1 compared with usual care (between-group difference, −3.5). Total fatigue remained lower in the intervention group at T2 (between-group difference, −2.4), but not at T3. Positive intervention effects were seen on physical and role functioning at T1 (between-group differences, 3.8 and 9.2, respectively) and in global health status/quality of life (between-group difference, 9.5), but not in social, emotional or cognitive functioning.

"The REFUEL trial demonstrated a statistically significant and clinically meaningful effect of a 12-week multidisciplinary intervention on fatigue in lymphoma survivors with persistent fatigue several years after treatment," the authors write.

Several authors disclosed ties to the pharmaceutical industry.

Publication details

Synne-Kristin H. Bøhn et al., Effect of a Multidisciplinary Intervention on Fatigue in Lymphoma Survivors With Persistent Fatigue: A Randomized Controlled Trial (the REFUEL trial), Journal of Clinical Oncology (2026). DOI: 10.1200/jco-26-00414

item.title: Half of adults in long COVID study report difficulty breathing 4 years later
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important findings on long COVID symptoms with clear implications for patient care.

Half of adults in long COVID study report difficulty breathing 4 years later

Half of adults in a new long COVID study reported symptoms that suggested dysfunctional breathing more than four years after their initial infection. Those with persistent breathing problems tended to be younger and female, and they were less likely to be hospitalized during acute COVID infection.

Dysfunctional breathing is an umbrella term for altered or abnormal breathing patterns such as rapid or shallow breathing that can lead to shortness of breath. The condition is associated with a high long COVID symptom burden overall.

For the study, published in Respiratory Research, a team led by researchers at Karolinska University Hospital in Stockholm, Sweden, analyzed data from 288 participants diagnosed as having long COVID.

Of those, half (143) had dysfunctional breathing four years after their initial COVID infection, as indicated by elevated Nijmegen questionnaire (NQ) scores. The NQ is a self-reported screening tool used to assess functional respiratory symptoms. NQ scores range from 0 to 64 and, for this study, an elevated score was defined as 23 or greater.

38% reported rapid heart rate upon standing

At an initial baseline visit after getting COVID (May 2020 to December 2022), participants who later scored 23 or above on the NQ walked significantly shorter distances on the six-minute walking test than those with lower scores, completed fewer repetitions on a one-minute sit-to-stand test and had weaker muscle contraction when inhaling. Standard lung-function measures were similar between groups.

At the 2024 follow-up, participants who were not hospitalized during acute COVID infection had about six times higher odds of scoring 23 or above on the NQ. Younger age, greater shortness of breath at the initial assessment and a lower volume of air exhaled in the first second of a lung-function test were also independent predictors of dysfunctional breathing.

Factors independently associated with higher odds of scoring 23 or above at follow-up include more severe shortness of breath and more long COVID and depression symptoms. Thirty-eight percent of those with scores of 23 and above reported a diagnosis of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), compared with 8% in those with lower scores. A higher proportion of those with NQ scores of 23 and greater were on sick leave than those with lower scores (44% vs. 14%).

POTS causes an abnormally rapid heart rate when moving from lying down or sitting to standing up, with no substantial drop in blood pressure.

Need for studies combining patient-reported, objective measures

The response rate at follow-up was moderate, note the researchers, and nonresponse bias can't be ruled out. "Individuals with ongoing symptoms may have been more likely to participate, while those without persistent symptoms may have been less likely to respond to the follow-up survey," they write. At the same time, those with severe symptoms may be underrepresented because the burden of completing the follow-up questionnaire was too great.

They conclude, "These findings demonstrate a substantial burden of persistent functional respiratory complaints but should not be interpreted as evidence of clinically confirmed dysfunctional breathing." They call for future studies that combine patient-reported assessments with objective measures of breathing patterns and lung function.

Publication details

Carl Hallberg et al., Predictors and prevalence of symptoms suggestive of dysfunctional breathing four years after COVID-19: a prospective observational study, Respiratory Research (2026). DOI: 10.1186/s12931-026-03996-6

Journal information: Respiratory Research

item.title: Ecuadorian plant shows potential to control bacteria in food
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Exploration of a potential new application for a traditional plant in food safety, with clear results.

Ecuadorian plant shows potential to control bacteria in food

A plant traditionally used by Indigenous communities in Ecuador could have a new application: helping control bacteria in ready-to-eat foods. A study published in the journal Foods found that extracts of Piper carpunya, locally known as guaviduca, reduced the presence of Clostridium perfringens in a refrigerated risotto food model.

The extract prepared using a mixture of water and ethanol reduced bacterial levels approximately 100-fold compared with contaminated food without the extract. Previous research had already identified antimicrobial activity in P. carpunya, but its effectiveness when incorporated directly into food had yet to be evaluated.

The research team tested three types of extracts obtained from the plant's leaves against 20 microorganisms associated with foodborne illnesses and food spoilage. Eight microorganisms showed some degree of susceptibility, including C. perfringens, a bacterium capable of producing toxins and causing food poisoning.

The researchers then moved beyond laboratory testing by incorporating the most promising extracts into precooked risotto, which was stored at 5°C for 30 days. Some samples were deliberately inoculated with C. perfringens to determine whether the antimicrobial effect could be maintained within the food.

The most significant result was observed with the hydroethanolic extract, prepared using equal parts ethanol and water. In the contaminated risotto, it produced an approximately 2-log reduction in C. perfringens levels compared with the control group by day seven, equivalent to a roughly 100-fold decrease. From day 15 onward, the bacterium was no longer detectable in those samples.

The same extract also reduced other bacterial groups used as indicators of food spoilage. "Our aim is to develop natural additives that offer functionality similar to that of artificial additives, while allowing their incorporation into clean-label products," said Felipe Reyes Bueno, a researcher at Universidad Técnica Particular de Loja (UTPL) and an author of the study. Although previous studies had identified antioxidant properties in P. carpunya extracts, the extracts exhibited a pro-oxidant effect when incorporated into risotto.

Nevertheless, malondialdehyde concentrations, an indicator of lipid oxidation, remained below 0.35 mg/kg throughout the 30-day storage period, lower than levels associated with perceptible rancidity. P. carpunya is not yet ready for use as a food preservative. The study was conducted using a risotto food model with an extract concentration of 8% and did not include chemical characterization or sensory evaluation of the extracts.

The researchers now aim to identify the compounds responsible for the observed antimicrobial activity, optimize the concentration required to achieve the desired effect and assess how the extract influences the taste and other sensory characteristics of the food. "We still need to study the stability of the extracts, further refine the experiment and investigate in greater depth the extraction methods for the compounds responsible for this antimicrobial activity," the researcher added.

More information

Jorge F. Reyes et al., Evaluating the Potential of Piper carpunya Extracts: Antimicrobial and Antioxidant Effects in a Risotto Food Model, Foods (2026). DOI: 10.3390/foods15152762

Source: Medical Xpress | Published: 2026-11-26 00:50 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Culturally relevant nutrition interventions can engage Black adults more effectively
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Insightful study on engaging Black adults in nutrition interventions with clear cultural considerations.

Culturally relevant nutrition interventions can engage Black adults more effectively

A recent study in the Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior explored how researchers can better engage Black adults with hypertension in digital nutrition interventions designed to improve dietary habits and reduce cardiovascular risk.

Researchers interviewed 30 Black adults (16 male) with hypertension about their interest in a digital nutrition program and their preferences for research recruitment. Participants expressed strong interest in an intervention that could help them improve their overall health, build healthy eating and cooking skills and receive guidance and accountability from a registered dietitian.

The findings highlighted the importance of culturally relevant recruitment materials featuring Black adults across ages, genders and body sizes, along with appealing healthy foods and the technology used in the intervention. Participants also emphasized that dietitians should understand Black cultural food traditions and lived experiences, noting that cultural competence was more important than the dietitian's race alone.

"Engaging Black adults in nutrition research requires more than simply sharing information about a study," said lead investigator Loneke T. Blackman Carr, Ph.D., RD, Department of Nutritional Sciences, University of Connecticut, Storrs, Connecticut. "Recruitment materials should reflect people's lived experiences, and researchers should consider the trusted community spaces and digital platforms people use in their daily lives. Just as importantly, nutrition professionals must understand the cultural and social contexts that shape food choices to help participants make meaningful changes to their health."

Participants identified both digital platforms, such as social media and YouTube, and trusted community spaces, including churches, as valuable places to share recruitment materials. Preferences varied somewhat by sex: women placed greater emphasis on traditional community settings, while men prioritized digital platforms.

These findings suggest that combining culturally relevant messaging with recruitment through familiar community spaces and digital channels may help researchers better engage Black adults, resulting in their greater representation in nutrition research.

Publication details

Loneke T. Blackman Carr et al., Paths to Participation With Black Adults: Identifying Recruitment Preferences and Interest in a Digital Nutrition Intervention to Reduce Hypertension, Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.jneb.2026.08.001

Journal information: Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior
